title: Data-Independent Acquisition Analysis to Identify Serum Biomarkers and Neoantigens for Differentiating Colorectal Cancer from Inflammatory Bowel Disease
projectDescription: Early detection of colorectal cancer (CRC) and distinguishing inflammatory bowel diseases from cancerous conditions significantly improve survival rates. While colonoscopy is the gold standard for CRC detection, it is invasive and associated with potential complications. Therefore, there is a need for blood biomarkers that possess high sensitivity and specificity which can be used for pre-diagnosis. In this study, we screened for serum biomarkers specifically altered in colonoscopy-positive (CP) patients (cancer group) when compared to colonoscopy-negative (CN) patients (suffering from other bowel-related illnesses with symptoms similar to CRC), and healthy control (HC) individuals (n=20 each). Using Data-Independent Acquisition-Mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) analysis, we identified potential protein markers and neoantigens uniquely altered in the CP group compared to the CN group.
sampleProcessingProtocol: An equal volume of diluted serum samples was taken from all the sample groups and subjected to protein precipitation by adding 5X volume of chilled acetone and incubating overnight at -20 °C. After incubation, the samples were centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 15 min to obtain the protein pellet, which was subsequently resuspended in 50 mM TEAB. Following the vendor protocol, protein concentrations in all samples were estimated using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Catalog number: 23225, Thermo Scientific). The protein amount was confirmed and normalized by running in SDS-PAGE. An equal amount of protein from each sample was reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 60 °C for 30 min. Following reduction, the samples were alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. The proteins were then digested with trypsin at a 1:20 (Protease: Protein) ratio and incubated at 37 °C for 18 hrs. Digestion was verified by visualizing the samples on an SDS-PAGE gel. The tryptic digests were subsequently desalted using SepPak C18 Cartridges (Part no: WAT054955, Waters) to remove any salts. The eluted peptides were quantified using the Pierce™ Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (Catalog number: 23275, Thermo Scientific) following the vendor's protocol.
dataProcessingProtocol: Based on peptide quantification, 2 µg/µL of peptides were analyzed using DIA on an EASY nLC 1200 nano liquid chromatography connected to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Bremen, Germany). Each sample was resuspended with 0.1% formic acid (FA) and spiked with 200 fmol of the PierceTM peptide retention time calibration mixture (Catalog number: 88320, Thermo Scientific) before loading onto a 96-well plate. Full MS scans captured peptide precursors in the 300-1500 m/z range using the Orbitrap with a resolution of 120,000. The automatic gain control (AGC) and maximum injection time (Max. IT) were set to 1.0e6 and 20 ms, respectively. Quadrupole-isolated precursors were fragmented using higher energy collision-induced dissociation (HCD) with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 32 ± 3%. Fragment ions were then acquired in the Orbitrap at 30,000 resolution with AGC and Max. IT of 1.0e6 and 54 ms, respectively. The raw files were analyzed using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) in library-free mode, with searches against the FASTA sequence from the Human Uniprot canonical and isoform database. Trypsin/P was chosen as the protease enzyme, allowing for one missed cleavage. Carbamidomethylation at cysteine was set as a fixed modification, while oxidation at methionine and acetylation at the N-terminus were specified as dynamic modifications.
